description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for the combination of features: leaves and flowering stems all basal, leaf laminae terete or subterete, less than 2 mm wide dorsiventrally; leaves 25–75 cm long, flowering stems 30–80 cm long and 1–1.5 mm wide.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria gracilis, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria gracilis [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for the combination of features: leaves and stems all basal, leaves almost terete, 8–30 cm long, apex recurved; culms 9–30 cm long and 0.5–1 mm wide; inflorescence of 3–25 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria humilis, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria humilis [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for the moderately wide leaf laminae (5–10 mm wide dorsiventrally), with the leaf and stem margins smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria laevis, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria laevis [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for often forming small dense ‘cushions’ raised above the soil surface; the stems leafy and branching, covered by imbricate bases of crowded leaves; internodes 0.2–0.5 cm long; stilt-roots often present.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria polyphylla, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria polyphylla [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for the leafy branching stems forming tangled or trailing masses to 50(–80) cm high; internodes mostly 7–12 cm long; leaves 1.5–3 mm dorsiventrally.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria prolifera, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria prolifera [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinctive among Anarthria species for the broad leaf laminae (5–10 mm wide dorsiventrally) and the leaf and stem margins coarsely or minutely scabrid.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria scabra, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria scabra [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Shortly rhizomatous but forming large dense tussocks of culms crowded on short rhizomes; cataphylls tan-brown, glossy, culms slender and flexible when fresh, to 1–1.5 (–1.8) mm diam. near the base, 0.5–1 m high, each with a compact ovoid or cylindrical spike with rigid glumes.
bibliographicCitation: B.G. Briggs, C.L. Connelly, S.L. Krauss (2019) Ecdeiocolea monostachya, in P.G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Ecdeiocolea monostachya [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from species of Ecdeiocolea by the culms consisting of several internodes; sheaths caducous, leaving swollen nodes; culms with (1–) 2–3 ovoid spikelets; trimerous flowers with tepals and stamens 6; trilocular ovary with 3 styles; fruit a capsule.
bibliographicCitation: B.G. Briggs, C.L. Connelly &, S.L. Krauss (2020) Georgeantha hexandra, in P.G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Georgeantha hexandra [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from other Lygin species by the plants not caespitose but forming patches of widely spaced culms or small groups of culms connected by long rhizomes; culm sheaths and inflorescence spathes ciliate with stiff hairs.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Lyginia barbata, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Lyginia barbata [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from Lyginia barbata by the plants caespitose with crowded culms; culm sheaths and spathes glabrous or sparsely or strongly ciliate; and from L. imberbis by the culms longer (50–150 cm tall), internodes longer (14–25 cm), and fertile spathes each subtending 1–3 flowers.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs (2018) Lyginia excelsa, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Lyginia excelsa [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from Lyginia barbata by the plants being caespitose with crowded culms; culm sheaths and inflorescence spathes glabrous or sparsely or strongly ciliate; and from L. excelsa by the culms shorter (30–100 cm tall), internodes shorter (5–11 cm), and fertile spathes each subtending a single flower.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Lyginia imberbis, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Lyginia imberbis [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from Restionaceae by the tetrathecate, bilocular anthers and pollen grains with graminoid annulus, and from other Anarthriaceae and most other Poales by the presence of well-developed equitant leaves.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Anarthria, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Culms unbranched, terete, striate; leaves reduced to a single scarious sheath; inflorescence of a single terminal compact cylindrical or ovoid spike, with zones of female and male flowers alternating once or twice along spike axis; glumes rigid, glumes and flowers spirally arranged in 5 ranks, on very short pedicels.
bibliographicCitation: B.G. Briggs, C.L. Connelly, S.L. Krauss (2019) Ecdeiocolea, in P.G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Ecdeiocolea [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Distinguished from Ecdeiocolea by the culms consisting of several internodes; inflorescence of 2 or 3 spikelets; trimerous flowers with tepals and stamens 6; trilocular ovary with 3 styles and fruit a capsule. Culms with 1–3 compact ovoid spikes, with zones of female and male flowers alternating along the spike axis; glumes rigid.
bibliographicCitation: B.G. Briggs, C.L. Connelly, S.L. Krauss (2020) Georgeantha, in P.G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Georgeantha [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Similar in habit to many Restionaceae but distinctive in the filaments of male flowers connate forming a stout column, the anthers 4-lobed and the seeds with fine short spines and an encircling hyaline flange.All Lygin species have similar seed morphology, a type not found elsewhere in the Anarthriaceae or Restionaceae.
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs, Carolyn L. Connelly & Siegfried L. Krauss (2018) Lyginia, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Lyginia [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Anarthriaceae are distinguished from Restionaceae by the tetrathecate, bilocular anthers and pollen grains with graminoid annulus, and from most other Poales by the presence of either a sclerenchyma cylinder bordered externally by a parenchyma sheath (a target=_blank href=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Lyginia rel=nofollow><span style=color:#800080>Lygin</span></a></b>, <b><a target=_blank href=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Hopkinsia rel=nofollow><span style=color:#800080>Hopkins</span></a></b>) or well-developed equitant leaves (<b><a target=_blank href=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthria rel=nofollow><span style=color:#800080>Anarthr</span></a></b>).
bibliographicCitation: Barbara G. Briggs (2018) Anarthriaceae, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Anarthriaceae [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Aphanopetalaceae are scrambling or climbing shrubs (often seen as woody vines) with prominently lenticellate stems, opposite leaves with minute stipules, and axillary flowers. The flowers are 4-merous, with four large sepals that enlarge as the fruit develops, and the petals are minute or absent. The gynoecium is 4-carpellate, with a partly inferior ovary, and the fruit is nut-like and 1-seeded.
bibliographicCitation: Val Stajsic (2018) Aphanopetalaceae, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Aphanopetalaceae [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Culms unbranched, with 1–3 distal inflorescence branches (if only one branch (peduncle) this is continuous with the culm but more slender), terete, striate; leaves reduced to scarious sheaths; sheath overlapping at the base; inflorescence of one or few compact cylindrical or ovoid spikes terminating culm or inflorescence branches; spikes with zones of female and male flowers alternating once or twice along spike axis, the basal zones mostly female; flowers spirally arranged in 5 ranks, on very short pedicels.
bibliographicCitation: B.G. Briggs (2019) Ecdeiocoleaceae, in P.G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Ecdeiocoleaceae [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]

description: Emblingiaceae are prostrate subshrubs with axillary, ebracteolate and strongly zygomorphic flowers. The corolla is a hood-shaped structure (calceolus) formed from 2 petals. The calceolus faces downward, changing orientation during development so that it is presented to the pollinator as being inverted. Androgynophore present. Nectary gland present, enclosed by a small pocket formed by the calceolus at the base. Androecium appearing as 4 fertile anthers and (3–) 6 staminodes.
bibliographicCitation: Val Stajsic (2018) Emblingiaceae, in Phillip G. Kodela (ed.)Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra. https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Emblingiaceae [Date Accessed: 02 December 2020]
